To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intranasal application of PG is effective in suppressing PGIA and that this effect is dependent on the continuous administration of the antigen, which is necessary to maintain tolerance.

(i) nasal administration of PG is an effective way of inducing tolerance to PG in mice, (ii) the tolerizing effect is maintained in adoptively transferred PGIA in SCID mice, (iii) the tolerized state is not maintained if PG is not continuously administered to SCID mice, and (iv) the tolerized cells are not effective in suppressing the disease if transferred into SCID mice that are not treated with PG.

(1) intranasal administration of PG is effective in preventing the development of arthritis in genetically predisposed mice; (2) intranasal treatment of PGIA in SCID mice requires continuous exposure to PG antigen to maintain tolerance; and (3) intranasal PG administration to SCID mice with PGIA is ineffective when the transferred lymphocytes are from non‐tolerate animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the induction of mucosal tolerance to a major macromolecular target antigen of autoimmune arthritis.
the mechanisms of oral tolerance, and the potential of this approach for treatment of autoimmune arthritis.
the development of a mucosal treatment for autoimmune arthritis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the continuous presence of antigen is critical in maintaining tolerance in the autoimmune arthritic model in SCID mice.
mucosal treatment of PGIA is effective in preventing disease development, but only if it is applied before the development of disease and continued for a prolonged time.
continuous antigen administration is critical for maintaining tolerance in adoptively‐transferred autoimmune arthritis in SCIDs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mucosal tolerance is an efficient way to prevent the development of PGIA.
the tolerogenic state can be established in adoptive transferred autoimmune arthritis in immunodeficient mice, but only if continuous nasal administration of the antigen is maintained.
the continuous nasal administration of antigen to maintain tolerance is critical to prevent the re‐activation of autoimmune arthritis in adoptively transferred disease in SCID mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mucosal treatment is most effective when it is started before the development of the disease.

mucosal tolerance induction requires continuous antigen supply to the nasal mucosa, and that the tolerized immune cells may not be stable and can revert to a pro‐arthritic state when antigen supply is discontinued.
mucosal treatment of arthritis is only effective when the antigen is continuously available at the mucosal surface.
